entities.summary:
Ban Yong (c. 50 CE – 150 CE), a distinguished military commander and diplomat of the Eastern Han dynasty, played a pivotal role in temporarily reasserting Chinese suzerainty over the Western Regions (modern Xinjiang and parts of Central Asia) during the early 2nd century CE. As the son of the legendary General Ban Chao and nephew to the esteemed historian Ban Gu, Yong inherited a formidable legacy of military prowess and scholarly acumen. His campaigns and diplomatic efforts were crucial in a period when Han influence west of the Hexi Corridor had significantly waned, marking a final, albeit brief, resurgence of imperial power in a strategically vital frontier during the Classical era.

Following decades of Han withdrawal and a resurgent Northern Xiongnu presence, Ban Yong embarked on his decisive campaigns beginning around 123 CE. Appointed as the Chief Clerk of the Western Regions, he led a force of Chinese and allied troops, systematically defeating Xiongnu remnants and re-establishing alliances with numerous oasis states such as Turfan and Khotan. His most notable achievement was the restoration of the Protectorate General of the Western Regions in 127 CE, an administrative and military apparatus that had been abandoned for over a decade. This re-establishment solidified Han control over key segments of the Silk Road, ensuring the flow of goods and tribute, and projecting Han power deep into Central Asia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ban Yong's campaigns and diplomatic efforts temporarily restored Han influence over the Western Regions in the 2nd century CE, securing vital sections of the Silk Road and ensuring continued East-West interaction during a period of imperial decline. His actions represent the last major Han effort to project power deep into Central Asia, impacting subsequent Chinese foreign policy.
